content: In clinical settings, the appropriate use of uterotonics is essential. Oral misoprostol is the preferred uterotonic in these scenarios due to its effectiveness and practicality. The dissemination and implementation of these recommendations require the involvement of all stakeholders at international, national, and local levels. It is critical to enhance women's access to maternal healthcare and to strengthen the capacity of healthcare facilities to provide high-quality services for all women during childbirth. These recommendations must be integrated into care packages and programs at the country and healthcare facility levels where applicable. A concise document summarizing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations, and research priorities will be prepared for public dissemination. This document will include annexes with detailed information such as methods, Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks, and Summary of Findings (SoF) tables for reference. WHO will also develop derivative tools to facilitate understanding and adaptation of these recommendations to local contexts, including a policy brief on postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) prevention, an updated PPH prevention clinical algorithm, and an online interactive platform on PPH prevention. The recommendations and tools will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. They will also be made available on the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research website and through the HRP News platform, which currently has over 4,500 subscribers, including clinicians, health program managers, policymakers, and service users worldwide. Updated recommendations will also be shared during meetings and scientific conferences attended by WHO maternal and perinatal health staff. The executive summary and recommendations will be translated into six United Nations languages for broader dissemination. Technical assistance will be provided to WHO regional offices interested in translating these recommendations into additional languages. National and subnational working groups should assess current guidelines and determine whether new guidelines or updates to existing ones are needed in alignment with these WHO recommendations. WHO staff, international agency partners, and professional societies can support national stakeholders in developing or revising guidelines and optimizing their implementation. The successful introduction of evidence-based policies for PPH prevention and management depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. These processes may involve developing or revising national guidelines and engaging all relevant stakeholders, including skilled health personnel. The recommendations should be tailored to suit the specific needs of each country and healthcare service, with any modifications justified transparently. An enabling environment should be created to support the implementation of these recommendations, including education to promote behavior change among skilled health personnel and ensure the use of evidence-based practices. National health systems must ensure the availability of high-quality uterotonics and necessary equipment wherever maternity services are provided. This includes establishing robust regulatory, procurement, and logistics processes to ensure medicines and equipment are obtained, transported, and stored correctly. Skilled health personnel working in childbirth settings require training and supportive supervision to use uterotonics appropriately and safely and to counsel women on the risks and benefits of available uterotonics. In settings where new uterotonics are introduced or practices are changed, additional training and monitoring may be necessary. Special attention should be given to correct dosage and safe use of uterotonics for PPH prevention, and efforts should be made to prevent their misuse for other indications. In settings where task shifting has been introduced for uterotonic administration, healthcare stakeholders should consider the needs of cadres administering uterotonics, such as community health workers, including drug supplies, access to referral systems, training, and supervision. Local professional societies and training institutions can play a significant role in implementation, and an inclusive and participatory process should be encouraged. Procurement agencies at all levels should procure only quality-certified uterotonic medicines. For example, oxytocin should be procured in single-use ampoules or vials of 10 international units (IU), labeled for storage at 2–8°C, and stored in refrigeration to prevent degradation and maintain quality, regardless of labeling. In settings with limited or inconsistent electricity, the use of misoprostol or heat-stable carbetocin may be more feasible, provided heat-stable carbetocin is locally available at a comparable cost to other effective uterotonics. Ergometrine or methylergometrine is contraindicated in women with hypertensive disorders and should only be used where women can be screened for these conditions. Programs implementing uterotonics for PPH prevention should ensure women are adequately informed about the need for uterotonics, available options, potential side effects, and their right to choose their care. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified key knowledge gaps requiring primary research. These include understanding the outcomes valued by women and their families regarding PPH prevention interventions, the effects of uterotonics on breastfeeding, maternal well-being, skin-to-skin contact, and mother-baby bonding, and determining the most effective dose and route of administration for uterotonics by mode of birth. Research is also needed on strategies to promote sustainable use of uterotonics, cost-effectiveness of different options in lowand middle-income countries, and the optimal intravenous oxytocin regimen for cesarean sections. Implementing these recommendations requires resources for sustainable procurement and storage of uterotonic drugs. Updating training curricula and providing training on the recommendations will enhance their impact and facilitate implementation. Standardizing care by incorporating these recommendations into intrapartum and immediate postpartum care packages can encourage behavior change among healthcare providers. Monitoring and evaluating the implementation and impact of these recommendations will occur at health-service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality. WHO's Standards for improving quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities provides prioritized measures to define quality of care criteria and indicators aligned with local targets. Data on implementation will be collected and evaluated to assess their impact on national policies. Interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based audits may be used to gather relevant data on interventions. WHO recommends using prophylactic uterotonic coverage as a process indicator for monitoring PPH prevention. This indicator assesses adherence to key recommendations and provides insights into the quality of care related to PPH prevention and treatment. Monitoring the quality of uterotonic drugs in low-resource settings can guide health personnel in selecting the most effective options. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) regularly reviews WHO's maternal and perinatal health recommendations to prioritize updates. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendations will be updated. If no new information is identified, the recommendations may be revalidated. Concerns about the validity of any recommendation will be promptly addressed, and updates will be made as needed. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
